document.content:
# vLLM #34752: checkpoint KV-cache quantization and CLI overrides disagree

- Status at capture: open
- Upstream: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/34752
- Pinned source: `vllm@272abd5f486967f1fb9db7ca7504f8c34235ef50`

Some checkpoints declare `kv_cache_quant_algo`. With those checkpoints,
`--kv-cache-dtype auto` incorrectly falls back to the model dtype instead of
the declared FP8 cache format, while an explicit `bfloat16` override reaches an
unsupported cache path and fails later.

Acceptance criteria:

1. Unit tests cover a checkpoint with and without `kv_cache_quant_algo`.
2. `auto` resolves consistently whether it was explicit or implicit.
3. An explicit override is either supported end to end or rejected early with
   an actionable configuration error.
4. The implementation documents the precedence of checkpoint metadata and CLI
   configuration.

    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"Quantization profile matrix for SLO tiers (fast / standard / cost-efficient)\",\n  \"space\": \"applied-ml-and-evals\",\n  \"author\": \"Arjun Desai\",\n  \"owner_team\": \"engineering\",\n  \"status\": \"published\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-01-15\",\n  \"last_updated\": \"2026-02-20\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Jonas Weber\",\n    \"Claire Dubois\",\n    \"Hassan Mirza\",\n    \"Sofia Ivanova\",\n    \"Allison Grant\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"quantization\",\n    \"inference\",\n    \"slo-tiers\",\n    \"batching\",\n    \"perf\",\n    \"evals\"\n  ],\n  \"confidentiality\": \"internal\",\n  \"related_pages\": [\n    \"confluence://eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/latency-slo-tiers-definition-fast-standard-cost-efficient\",\n    \"confluence://eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/workload-aware-batching-defaults-design\",\n    \"confluence://applied-ml-and-evals/quality-guardrails/quality-checks-for-quantization-and-batching\",\n    \"confluence://eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/batching-slo-tier-benchmark-methodology\"\n  ],\n  \"body\": \"## Purpose\\nThis page defines Redwood\\u2019s *recommended quantization variants* per **latency SLO tier** (fast / standard / cost-efficient) and **model family**, and documents the **compatibility constraints** between quantization and the new workload-aware batching defaults.\\n\\nThis is intentionally a *matrix of supported, production-recommended choices* (not an exhaustive list of all quantizers). It is used by:\\n- Model catalog metadata (\\\"recommended profiles\\\")\\n- Runtime defaults for tiered batching (avoid unsafe/unsupported combos)\\n- Console \\u201crecommended tier/profile\\u201d explanations\\n- Perf canary and benchmark gating configuration\\n\\n## Non-goals\\n- Per-tenant online auto-tuning (out of scope for initial tiered batching launch)\\n- Model-by-model micro-optimizations beyond the listed families\\n\\n## Definitions\\n**Tier (customer-facing):**\\n- **fast**: prioritize tail latency and stable streaming cadence.\\n- **standard**: balanced latency and throughput.\\n- **cost-efficient**: maximize throughput / lowest $/1K tokens while remaining within published SLOs.\\n\\n**Quantization variants (naming used in model catalog + runtime):**\\n- **bf16**: baseline high-quality, higher memory footprint.\\n- **fp16**: similar to bf16, used on some older kernels; prefer bf16 when supported.\\n- **w8a16 (int8 weight-only)**: weights int8, activations bf16/fp16.\\n- **w4a16 (int4 weight-only, AWQ/GPTQ-class)**: weights int4, activations bf16/fp16; best cost, higher risk.\\n- **fp8 (fp8 compute / or weight+activation fp8 depending on kernel)**: hardware-dependent (primarily H100); strong perf, can be sensitive on some tasks.\\n- **kv8 (KV cache fp8)**: KV cache stored in fp8 (or similar reduced precision), reduces memory pressure and improves batching headroom; may affect quality in edge cases.\\n\\n**Batching defaults (scheduler knobs affected):** max_wait_ms, max_batch_tokens, max_batch_size, admission control/backpressure, prefill/decode balancing.\\n\\n## Quick guidance (what to pick)\\n- **fast**: prefer **bf16** (or **w8a16** only when it does not regress p99/stream cadence on the target hardware/model).\\n- **standard**: prefer **w8a16** (or **bf16** when model is sensitive or kernels are unstable).\\n- **cost-efficient**: prefer **w4a16** *or* **fp8** (H100) *plus* optional **kv8** when needed to prevent memory-bound batching collapse.\\n\\n## Compatibility constraints with tiered batching defaults\\nThe tiered batching project makes some combinations either unsupported or strongly discouraged because they create \\u201cfoot-guns\\u201d under mixed workloads.\\n\\n### 1) Streaming stability (fast tier)\\n- Streaming endpoints are more sensitive to **decode-time jitter** (kernel variance + queueing).\\n- Quantization variants that introduce sporadic dequant overhead or kernel fallback can cause *visible token cadence variability* even when average latency is acceptable.\\n- **Rule:** For **fast + streaming**, only variants listed as \\u201c\\u2705 fast-safe streaming\\u201d in the matrix are supported by default.\\n\\n### 2) Prefill memory headroom (cost-efficient tier)\\n- Cost-efficient uses larger batches and higher max_batch_tokens; prefill is frequently memory-bound.\\n- Aggressive quantization can help (smaller weights), but **KV cache often dominates** for long contexts.\\n- **Rule:** If peak KV memory is the limiting factor (detected by runtime signals), allow **kv8** (KV cache reduced precision) only for model families marked \\u201ckv8-compatible\\u201d.\\n\\n### 3) Kernel availability / fallback risk\\n- Some model families + quant modes require specific kernel paths; if a fallback path is triggered at runtime, latency SLOs become unpredictable.\\n- **Rule:** If kernel coverage is partial for a mode on a given GPU class, the runtime should not select it as a tier default; it may be available only as an explicit override with warnings.\\n\\n### 4) Mixed prompt-length + concurrency\\n- Under mixed workloads, low-precision modes can change the \\u201cbest\\u201d prefill/decode split and batch shaping.\\n- **Rule:** The scheduler assumes tier profiles were benchmarked against the quant variant. Do not mix unbenchmarked pairs (e.g., switching to w4a16 while keeping fast-tier wait budgets) without re-validation.\\n\\n### 5) Observability and reason codes\\nWhen the runtime does not apply the recommended quantization for a tier, it must emit a reason code:\\n- `model_constraint` (mode unsupported by model family)\\n- `hardware_constraint` (mode unsupported by GPU class)\\n- `tier_safety` (disallowed for tier, e.g., fast+streaming)\\n- `overload_mode` (temporary safety behavior)\\n- `customer_override` / `route_override`\\n\\n## Matrix: recommended quantization by model family and SLO tier\\nLegend:\\n- \\u2705 Recommended default\\n- \\u26a0\\ufe0f Allowed but not default (requires justification / expected trade-off)\\n- \\u274c Not supported for this tier as a default\\n- Notes call out batching constraints and required guardrails\\n\\n### GPU classes referenced\\n- **H100**: Hopper\\n- **A100**: Ampere\\n- **L4**: Ada (latency-focused, lower memory)\\n\\n### Model families in scope (initial release)\\n- Llama 3.x: 8B, 70B (dense)\\n- Mistral 7B (dense)\\n- Mixtral 8x7B / similar MoE (expert routing)\\n- Qwen2: 7B, 72B (dense)\\n\\n> If a model is not listed, default to **bf16** for fast, **w8a16** for standard, and require explicit perf+quality sign-off for cost-efficient.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Llama 3.x 8B (dense)\\n| Tier | H100 | A100 | L4 | fast-safe streaming | Batching constraints / notes |\\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\\n| fast | \\u2705 bf16 (or \\u26a0\\ufe0f w8a16) | \\u2705 bf16 (or \\u26a0\\ufe0f w8a16) | \\u2705 bf16 | \\u2705 bf16 | w8a16 allowed only if p99 and stream cadence pass gates; keep max_wait_ms tight. |\\n| standard | \\u2705 w8a16 | \\u2705 w8a16 | \\u26a0\\ufe0f w8a16 | \\u2705 w8a16 | L4: w8a16 can be throughput-positive but may reduce headroom for large concurrent streaming; monitor queue depth. |\\n| cost-efficient | \\u2705 fp8 (preferred) or \\u2705 w4a16 | \\u2705 w4a16 | \\u26a0\\ufe0f w4a16 | \\u26a0\\ufe0f (non-streaming preferred) | For L4 cost-efficient, cap max_batch_tokens to prevent OOM; prefer non-streaming. kv8 optional when long-context workloads dominate. |\\n\\n### Llama 3.x 70B (dense)\\n| Tier | H100 | A100 | L4 | fast-safe streaming | Batching constraints / notes |\\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\\n| fast | \\u2705 bf16 | \\u2705 bf16 | \\u274c (not recommended) | \\u2705 bf16 | Fast tier defaults assume stable decode; do not enable low-precision KV on fast unless explicitly approved. |\\n| standard | \\u2705 w8a16 | \\u2705 w8a16 | \\u274c | \\u2705 w8a16 | w8a16 increases batch headroom; still memory-bound for long context\\u2014watch KV growth. |\\n| cost-efficient | \\u2705 fp8 + \\u26a0\\ufe0f kv8 | \\u2705 w4a16 + \\u26a0\\ufe0f kv8 | \\u274c | \\u26a0\\ufe0f (non-streaming preferred) | kv8 is a lever for long-context, high concurrency; require quality guardrails on summarization and code tasks. |\\n\\n### Mistral 7B (dense)\\n| Tier | H100 | A100 | L4 | fast-safe streaming | Batching constraints / notes |\\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\\n| fast | \\u2705 bf16 | \\u2705 bf16 | \\u2705 bf16 | \\u2705 bf16 | Good baseline; stable streaming cadence. |\\n| standard | \\u2705 w8a16 | \\u2705 w8a16 | \\u2705 w8a16 | \\u2705 w8a16 | Generally safe; validate on tool-calling prompts for format sensitivity. |\\n| cost-efficient | \\u2705 fp8 or \\u2705 w4a16 | \\u2705 w4a16 | \\u26a0\\ufe0f w4a16 | \\u26a0\\ufe0f | w4a16 increases throughput; require structured output pass-rate checks (see guardrails). |\\n\\n### Mixtral 8x7B (MoE)\\n| Tier | H100 | A100 | L4 | fast-safe streaming | Batching constraints / notes |\\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\\n| fast | \\u2705 bf16 | \\u2705 bf16 | \\u274c | \\u2705 bf16 | MoE routing can amplify variance under quant; fast tier stays bf16. |\\n| standard | \\u26a0\\ufe0f w8a16 | \\u26a0\\ufe0f w8a16 | \\u274c | \\u26a0\\ufe0f | Allowed only where kernel coverage is verified; monitor tail latency under mixed prompt lengths. |\\n| cost-efficient | \\u26a0\\ufe0f fp8 (only with validated kernels) | \\u274c | \\u274c | \\u274c | MoE + aggressive quant often increases variance; only enable for specific deployments after perf+quality sign-off. |\\n\\n### Qwen2 7B (dense)\\n| Tier | H100 | A100 | L4 | fast-safe streaming | Batching constraints / notes |\\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\\n| fast | \\u2705 bf16 | \\u2705 bf16 | \\u2705 bf16 | \\u2705 bf16 | Fast tier uses bf16 to avoid format regressions in multilingual / instruction-following edge cases. |\\n| standard | \\u2705 w8a16 | \\u2705 w8a16 | \\u26a0\\ufe0f w8a16 | \\u2705 w8a16 | L4: confirm no p99 regression on short prompts with high concurrency. |\\n| cost-efficient | \\u2705 fp8 or \\u2705 w4a16 | \\u2705 w4a16 | \\u26a0\\ufe0f w4a16 | \\u26a0\\ufe0f | For heavy long-context: consider kv8; require multilingual prompt-set quality gates. |\\n\\n### Qwen2 72B (dense)\\n| Tier | H100 | A100 | L4 | fast-safe streaming | Batching constraints / notes |\\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\\n| fast | \\u2705 bf16 | \\u2705 bf16 | \\u274c | \\u2705 bf16 | Same as other 70B-class: do not default to low precision in fast. |\\n| standard | \\u2705 w8a16 | \\u2705 w8a16 | \\u274c | \\u2705 w8a16 | Standard defaults assume w8a16 kernels are stable; if not, fall back to bf16 and emit `hardware_constraint`. |\\n| cost-efficient | \\u2705 fp8 + \\u26a0\\ufe0f kv8 | \\u2705 w4a16 + \\u26a0\\ufe0f kv8 | \\u274c | \\u26a0\\ufe0f (non-streaming preferred) | For long context + high concurrency, kv8 can be required to avoid OOM with cost-efficient batch sizes; requires strict quality checks. |\\n\\n## Batching-default constraints by quant mode (operational checklist)\\nUse this when pairing tiered batching profiles with quantization.\\n\\n### bf16 / fp16\\n- Safest for fast-tier streaming.\\n- Highest memory usage; can constrain max_batch_tokens in cost-efficient.\\n- **Recommended batching posture:** smaller max_batch_tokens for large models; rely on scheduler admission control under burst.\\n\\n### w8a16 (int8 weight-only)\\n- Usually a strong default for standard tier.\\n- Potential risk: kernel fallback on some GPU/model combos; may introduce latency spikes.\\n- **Batching posture:** standard tier can increase max_batch_tokens moderately; keep fast tier conservative.\\n\\n### w4a16 (int4 weight-only)\\n- Best cost/throughput when kernels are robust.\\n- Higher risk for quality regressions on strict formatting tasks and some multilingual edge cases.\\n- **Batching posture:** cost-efficient can use larger batches, but must enforce queue depth guardrails to prevent \\u201cbatching runaway.\\u201d\\n\\n### fp8 (H100)\\n- Strong throughput for both prefill and decode on H100-class hardware.\\n- Quality is generally acceptable but requires tier-specific prompt-set validation.\\n- **Batching posture:** cost-efficient can push larger batches; ensure decode-time jitter is acceptable if used with streaming.\\n\\n### kv8 (reduced-precision KV cache)\\n- Primarily a memory headroom lever for long context.\\n- Can affect quality subtly (especially long multi-turn chats); requires targeted evals.\\n- **Batching posture:** enables higher max_batch_tokens without OOM; must be paired with strict regression detection (quality + latency).\\n\\n## Quality and safety requirements (must pass to be \\u201c\\u2705 Recommended\\u201d)\\nA quant mode is marked \\u2705 only if it passes:\\n- **Perf gates:** tier-specific latency targets in the benchmark methodology (p95/p99 as defined in SLO tier doc), plus streaming cadence stability checks where applicable.\\n- **Correctness:** no increased error rate (timeouts, OOMs, invalid outputs) beyond guardrail thresholds.\\n- **Quality guardrails:** see linked \\u201cquality checks\\u201d page. At minimum:\\n  - Structured output / tool-call format pass rate (no regression beyond agreed threshold)\\n  - Prompt-set win-rate or score regression below the allowed delta per task type\\n  - No increase in truncation-related failures attributable to batching/quant changes\\n\\n## How this matrix is used in product/runtime\\n1) **Catalog metadata:** each model advertises allowed quant profiles per GPU class.\\n2) **Tier default selection:** runtime chooses a tier profile that is valid for (model family, GPU class, endpoint mode [streaming/non-streaming]).\\n3) **Fallback behavior:** if a recommended profile is not available, runtime falls back in this order unless overridden:\\n   - cost-efficient: fp8 \\u2192 w4a16 \\u2192 w8a16 \\u2192 bf16\\n   - standard: w8a16 \\u2192 bf16\\n   - fast: bf16\\n4) **Telemetry:** always emit selection reason codes when falling back or applying overrides.\\n\\n## Change management\\n- Owner: Applied ML / Evals (Jonas Weber) + Runtime Scheduling (Sofia Ivanova) for any change that affects tier defaults.\\n- Any change to a \\u2705 recommendation requires:\\n  1. Updated benchmark run attached to the perf suite artifact\\n  2. Updated quality report for relevant prompt sets\\n  3. SRE sign-off if it changes fast-tier streaming behavior or affects telemetry cardinality\\n  4. Changelog entry in runtime release notes\\n\\n## Open items / known limitations (as of 2026-02-20)\\n- MoE families: limited recommended low-precision defaults due to higher variance and kernel coverage gaps.\\n- L4 cost-efficient: w4a16 supported only with conservative caps on max_batch_tokens; otherwise OOM risk under long contexts.\\n- kv8: allowed only on selected dense families; still collecting more long multi-turn chat eval evidence.\\n\\n## Appendix: FAQ\\n**Q: Does choosing a batching tier automatically change quantization?**\\nA: Not in the first release. Tier selects batching defaults; quantization follows model catalog \\u201crecommended profile\\u201d defaults and compatibility rules. Console may suggest a quant mode for cost-efficient but will not auto-apply without explicit configuration.\\n\\n**Q: Why is fast tier mostly bf16?**\\nA: Fast tier prioritizes predictable tail latency and stable streaming cadence. Even small kernel fallback risk or decode jitter can violate user-visible expectations.\\n\\n**Q: Can enterprise customers override this matrix?**\\nA: Yes, via route/tenant overrides (Dedicated/Private). Overrides are supported but must still satisfy \\u201callowed\\u201d constraints for the hardware/model; otherwise runtime will reject or fall back with reason codes.\\n\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"body\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_0e36881e8f2a4244b3f33e5906b1ed7c\"\n}",

document.title: Quantization profile matrix for SLO tiers (fast / standard / cost-efficient)
document.content:
{
  "title": "Quantization profile matrix for SLO tiers (fast / standard / cost-efficient)",
  "space": "applied-ml-and-evals",
  "author": "Arjun Desai",
  "owner_team": "engineering",
  "status": "published",
  "created_at": "2026-01-15",
  "last_updated": "2026-02-20",
  "reviewers": [
    "Jonas Weber",
    "Claire Dubois",
    "Hassan Mirza",
    "Sofia Ivanova",
    "Allison Grant"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "quantization",
    "inference",
    "slo-tiers",
    "batching",
    "perf",
    "evals"
  ],
  "confidentiality": "internal",
  "related_pages": [
    "confluence://eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/latency-slo-tiers-definition-fast-standard-cost-efficient",
    "confluence://eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/workload-aware-batching-defaults-design",
    "confluence://applied-ml-and-evals/quality-guardrails/quality-checks-for-quantization-and-batching",
    "confluence://eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/batching-slo-tier-benchmark-methodology"
  ],
  "body": "## Purpose
This page defines Redwood’s *recommended quantization variants* per **latency SLO tier** (fast / standard / cost-efficient) and **model family**, and documents the **compatibility constraints** between quantization and the new workload-aware batching defaults.

This is intentionally a *matrix of supported, production-recommended choices* (not an exhaustive list of all quantizers). It is used by:
- Model catalog metadata ("recommended profiles")
- Runtime defaults for tiered batching (avoid unsafe/unsupported combos)
- Console “recommended tier/profile” explanations
- Perf canary and benchmark gating configuration

## Non-goals
- Per-tenant online auto-tuning (out of scope for initial tiered batching launch)
- Model-by-model micro-optimizations beyond the listed families

## Definitions
**Tier (customer-facing):**
- **fast**: prioritize tail latency and stable streaming cadence.
- **standard**: balanced latency and throughput.
- **cost-efficient**: maximize throughput / lowest $/1K tokens while remaining within published SLOs.

**Quantization variants (naming used in model catalog + runtime):**
- **bf16**: baseline high-quality, higher memory footprint.
- **fp16**: similar to bf16, used on some older kernels; prefer bf16 when supported.
- **w8a16 (int8 weight-only)**: weights int8, activations bf16/fp16.
- **w4a16 (int4 weight-only, AWQ/GPTQ-class)**: weights int4, activations bf16/fp16; best cost, higher risk.
- **fp8 (fp8 compute / or weight+activation fp8 depending on kernel)**: hardware-dependent (primarily H100); strong perf, can be sensitive on some tasks.
- **kv8 (KV cache fp8)**: KV cache stored in fp8 (or similar reduced precision), reduces memory pressure and improves batching headroom; may affect quality in edge cases.

**Batching defaults (scheduler knobs affected):** max_wait_ms, max_batch_tokens, max_batch_size, admission control/backpressure, prefill/decode balancing.

## Quick guidance (what to pick)
- **fast**: prefer **bf16** (or **w8a16** only when it does not regress p99/stream cadence on the target hardware/model).
- **standard**: prefer **w8a16** (or **bf16** when model is sensitive or kernels are unstable).
- **cost-efficient**: prefer **w4a16** *or* **fp8** (H100) *plus* optional **kv8** when needed to prevent memory-bound batching collapse.

## Compatibility constraints with tiered batching defaults
The tiered batching project makes some combinations either unsupported or strongly discouraged because they create “foot-guns” under mixed workloads.

### 1) Streaming stability (fast tier)
- Streaming endpoints are more sensitive to **decode-time jitter** (kernel variance + queueing).
- Quantization variants that introduce sporadic dequant overhead or kernel fallback can cause *visible token cadence variability* even when average latency is acceptable.
- **Rule:** For **fast + streaming**, only variants listed as “✅ fast-safe streaming” in the matrix are supported by default.

### 2) Prefill memory headroom (cost-efficient tier)
- Cost-efficient uses larger batches and higher max_batch_tokens; prefill is frequently memory-bound.
- Aggressive quantization can help (smaller weights), but **KV cache often dominates** for long contexts.
- **Rule:** If peak KV memory is the limiting factor (detected by runtime signals), allow **kv8** (KV cache reduced precision) only for model families marked “kv8-compatible”.

### 3) Kernel availability / fallback risk
- Some model families + quant modes require specific kernel paths; if a fallback path is triggered at runtime, latency SLOs become unpredictable.
- **Rule:** If kernel coverage is partial for a mode on a given GPU class, the runtime should not select it as a tier default; it may be available only as an explicit override with warnings.

### 4) Mixed prompt-length + concurrency
- Under mixed workloads, low-precision modes can change the “best” prefill/decode split and batch shaping.
- **Rule:** The scheduler assumes tier profiles were benchmarked against the quant variant. Do not mix unbenchmarked pairs (e.g., switching to w4a16 while keeping fast-tier wait budgets) without re-validation.

### 5) Observability and reason codes
When the runtime does not apply the recommended quantization for a tier, it must emit a reason code:
- `model_constraint` (mode unsupported by model family)
- `hardware_constraint` (mode unsupported by GPU class)
- `tier_safety` (disallowed for tier, e.g., fast+streaming)
- `overload_mode` (temporary safety behavior)
- `customer_override` / `route_override`

## Matrix: recommended quantization by model family and SLO tier
Legend:
- ✅ Recommended default
- ⚠️ Allowed but not default (requires justification / expected trade-off)
- ❌ Not supported for this tier as a default
- Notes call out batching constraints and required guardrails

### GPU classes referenced
- **H100**: Hopper
- **A100**: Ampere
- **L4**: Ada (latency-focused, lower memory)

### Model families in scope (initial release)
- Llama 3.x: 8B, 70B (dense)
- Mistral 7B (dense)
- Mixtral 8x7B / similar MoE (expert routing)
- Qwen2: 7B, 72B (dense)

> If a model is not listed, default to **bf16** for fast, **w8a16** for standard, and require explicit perf+quality sign-off for cost-efficient.

---

### Llama 3.x 8B (dense)
| Tier | H100 | A100 | L4 | fast-safe streaming | Batching constraints / notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| fast | ✅ bf16 (or ⚠️ w8a16) | ✅ bf16 (or ⚠️ w8a16) | ✅ bf16 | ✅ bf16 | w8a16 allowed only if p99 and stream cadence pass gates; keep max_wait_ms tight. |
| standard | ✅ w8a16 | ✅ w8a16 | ⚠️ w8a16 | ✅ w8a16 | L4: w8a16 can be throughput-positive but may reduce headroom for large concurrent streaming; monitor queue depth. |
| cost-efficient | ✅ fp8 (preferred) or ✅ w4a16 | ✅ w4a16 | ⚠️ w4a16 | ⚠️ (non-streaming preferred) | For L4 cost-efficient, cap max_batch_tokens to prevent OOM; prefer non-streaming. kv8 optional when long-context workloads dominate. |

### Llama 3.x 70B (dense)
| Tier | H100 | A100 | L4 | fast-safe streaming | Batching constraints / notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| fast | ✅ bf16 | ✅ bf16 | ❌ (not recommended) | ✅ bf16 | Fast tier defaults assume stable decode; do not enable low-precision KV on fast unless explicitly approved. |
| standard | ✅ w8a16 | ✅ w8a16 | ❌ | ✅ w8a16 | w8a16 increases batch headroom; still memory-bound for long context—watch KV growth. |
| cost-efficient | ✅ fp8 + ⚠️ kv8 | ✅ w4a16 + ⚠️ kv8 | ❌ | ⚠️ (non-streaming preferred) | kv8 is a lever for long-context, high concurrency; require quality guardrails on summarization and code tasks. |

### Mistral 7B (dense)
| Tier | H100 | A100 | L4 | fast-safe streaming | Batching constraints / notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| fast | ✅ bf16 | ✅ bf16 | ✅ bf16 | ✅ bf16 | Good baseline; stable streaming cadence. |
| standard | ✅ w8a16 | ✅ w8a16 | ✅ w8a16 | ✅ w8a16 | Generally safe; validate on tool-calling prompts for format sensitivity. |
| cost-efficient | ✅ fp8 or ✅ w4a16 | ✅ w4a16 | ⚠️ w4a16 | ⚠️ | w4a16 increases throughput; require structured output pass-rate checks (see guardrails). |

### Mixtral 8x7B (MoE)
| Tier | H100 | A100 | L4 | fast-safe streaming | Batching constraints / notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| fast | ✅ bf16 | ✅ bf16 | ❌ | ✅ bf16 | MoE routing can amplify variance under quant; fast tier stays bf16. |
| standard | ⚠️ w8a16 | ⚠️ w8a16 | ❌ | ⚠️ | Allowed only where kernel coverage is verified; monitor tail latency under mixed prompt lengths. |
| cost-efficient | ⚠️ fp8 (only with validated kernels) | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | MoE + aggressive quant often increases variance; only enable for specific deployments after perf+quality sign-off. |

### Qwen2 7B (dense)
| Tier | H100 | A100 | L4 | fast-safe streaming | Batching constraints / notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| fast | ✅ bf16 | ✅ bf16 | ✅ bf16 | ✅ bf16 | Fast tier uses bf16 to avoid format regressions in multilingual / instruction-following edge cases. |
| standard | ✅ w8a16 | ✅ w8a16 | ⚠️ w8a16 | ✅ w8a16 | L4: confirm no p99 regression on short prompts with high concurrency. |
| cost-efficient | ✅ fp8 or ✅ w4a16 | ✅ w4a16 | ⚠️ w4a16 | ⚠️ | For heavy long-context: consider kv8; require multilingual prompt-set quality gates. |

### Qwen2 72B (dense)
| Tier | H100 | A100 | L4 | fast-safe streaming | Batching constraints / notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| fast | ✅ bf16 | ✅ bf16 | ❌ | ✅ bf16 | Same as other 70B-class: do not default to low precision in fast. |
| standard | ✅ w8a16 | ✅ w8a16 | ❌ | ✅ w8a16 | Standard defaults assume w8a16 kernels are stable; if not, fall back to bf16 and emit `hardware_constraint`. |
| cost-efficient | ✅ fp8 + ⚠️ kv8 | ✅ w4a16 + ⚠️ kv8 | ❌ | ⚠️ (non-streaming preferred) | For long context + high concurrency, kv8 can be required to avoid OOM with cost-efficient batch sizes; requires strict quality checks. |

## Batching-default constraints by quant mode (operational checklist)
Use this when pairing tiered batching profiles with quantization.

### bf16 / fp16
- Safest for fast-tier streaming.
- Highest memory usage; can constrain max_batch_tokens in cost-efficient.
- **Recommended batching posture:** smaller max_batch_tokens for large models; rely on scheduler admission control under burst.

### w8a16 (int8 weight-only)
- Usually a strong default for standard tier.
- Potential risk: kernel fallback on some GPU/model combos; may introduce latency spikes.
- **Batching posture:** standard tier can increase max_batch_tokens moderately; keep fast tier conservative.

### w4a16 (int4 weight-only)
- Best cost/throughput when kernels are robust.
- Higher risk for quality regressions on strict formatting tasks and some multilingual edge cases.
- **Batching posture:** cost-efficient can use larger batches, but must enforce queue depth guardrails to prevent “batching runaway.”

### fp8 (H100)
- Strong throughput for both prefill and decode on H100-class hardware.
- Quality is generally acceptable but requires tier-specific prompt-set validation.
- **Batching posture:** cost-efficient can push larger batches; ensure decode-time jitter is acceptable if used with streaming.

### kv8 (reduced-precision KV cache)
- Primarily a memory headroom lever for long context.
- Can affect quality subtly (especially long multi-turn chats); requires targeted evals.
- **Batching posture:** enables higher max_batch_tokens without OOM; must be paired with strict regression detection (quality + latency).

## Quality and safety requirements (must pass to be “✅ Recommended”)
A quant mode is marked ✅ only if it passes:
- **Perf gates:** tier-specific latency targets in the benchmark methodology (p95/p99 as defined in SLO tier doc), plus streaming cadence stability checks where applicable.
- **Correctness:** no increased error rate (timeouts, OOMs, invalid outputs) beyond guardrail thresholds.
- **Quality guardrails:** see linked “quality checks” page. At minimum:
  - Structured output / tool-call format pass rate (no regression beyond agreed threshold)
  - Prompt-set win-rate or score regression below the allowed delta per task type
  - No increase in truncation-related failures attributable to batching/quant changes

## How this matrix is used in product/runtime
1) **Catalog metadata:** each model advertises allowed quant profiles per GPU class.
2) **Tier default selection:** runtime chooses a tier profile that is valid for (model family, GPU class, endpoint mode [streaming/non-streaming]).
3) **Fallback behavior:** if a recommended profile is not available, runtime falls back in this order unless overridden:
   - cost-efficient: fp8 → w4a16 → w8a16 → bf16
   - standard: w8a16 → bf16
   - fast: bf16
4) **Telemetry:** always emit selection reason codes when falling back or applying overrides.

## Change management
- Owner: Applied ML / Evals (Jonas Weber) + Runtime Scheduling (Sofia Ivanova) for any change that affects tier defaults.
- Any change to a ✅ recommendation requires:
  1. Updated benchmark run attached to the perf suite artifact
  2. Updated quality report for relevant prompt sets
  3. SRE sign-off if it changes fast-tier streaming behavior or affects telemetry cardinality
  4. Changelog entry in runtime release notes

## Open items / known limitations (as of 2026-02-20)
- MoE families: limited recommended low-precision defaults due to higher variance and kernel coverage gaps.
- L4 cost-efficient: w4a16 supported only with conservative caps on max_batch_tokens; otherwise OOM risk under long contexts.
- kv8: allowed only on selected dense families; still collecting more long multi-turn chat eval evidence.

## Appendix: FAQ
**Q: Does choosing a batching tier automatically change quantization?**
A: Not in the first release. Tier selects batching defaults; quantization follows model catalog “recommended profile” defaults and compatibility rules. Console may suggest a quant mode for cost-efficient but will not auto-apply without explicit configuration.

**Q: Why is fast tier mostly bf16?**
A: Fast tier prioritizes predictable tail latency and stable streaming cadence. Even small kernel fallback risk or decode jitter can violate user-visible expectations.

**Q: Can enterprise customers override this matrix?**
A: Yes, via route/tenant overrides (Dedicated/Private). Overrides are supported but must still satisfy “allowed” constraints for the hardware/model; otherwise runtime will reject or fall back with reason codes.

    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/confluence",
    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"ADR-019: FP8/INT8 kernel auto-selection heuristics (Hosted Runtime)\",\n  \"space\": \"architecture-and-standards\",\n  \"author\": \"Noah Patel\",\n  \"owner_team\": \"engineering\",\n  \"status\": \"published\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-02-14\",\n  \"last_updated\": \"2026-02-26\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Hiro Tanaka\",\n    \"Sofia Ivanova\",\n    \"Rina Kobayashi\",\n    \"Jonas Weber\",\n    \"Claire Dubois\",\n    \"Rafael Mendes\",\n    \"Allison Grant\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"adr\",\n    \"serving-runtime\",\n    \"kernels\",\n    \"fp8\",\n    \"int8\",\n    \"autoselect\",\n    \"performance\",\n    \"rollout\"\n  ],\n  \"confidentiality\": \"internal\",\n  \"related_pages\": [\n    \"confluence://eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/kernel-benchmarking-methodology-top-hosted-models\",\n    \"confluence://applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles/fp8-int8-profile-policy-for-hosted-catalog\",\n    \"confluence://eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/perf-canary-rollout-for-new-kernels\",\n    \"confluence://architecture-and-standards/performance-standards/benchmarking-standards-fp8-int8\",\n    \"linear://ENG-7430-kernel-auto-selection-heuristics-implementation\",\n    \"linear://ENG-7426-perf-canary-thresholds-for-fp8-int8-rollout\"\n  ],\n  \"body\": \"## Status\\n**Accepted** (implemented behind flags; default-on gated by perf canary and eval sign-off).\\n\\n## Summary\\nThis ADR defines the runtime\\u2019s **kernel auto-selection heuristics** for choosing **FP8**, **INT8**, or **baseline (BF16/FP16)** kernel paths for attention and GEMMs during LLM inference. The heuristics are driven by:\\n- **GPU architecture** (H100/Hopper, A100/Ampere, L4/Ada where applicable)\\n- **Model shape** (hidden size, head dim, KV head dim, alignment constraints)\\n- **Sequence-length regime** (prefill vs decode; short vs long context)\\n- **Workload characteristics** (batch size, concurrency, and prefill/decode mix)\\n\\nThe decision includes:\\n- A prioritized selection order per GPU + workload regime\\n- Explicit **shape guardrails** (alignment, min/max dimensions)\\n- **Fallback rules** (correctness, unsupported shapes, quality gating)\\n- Rollout controls (flags, canary cohorts, and rollback triggers)\\n\\n## Context\\nRedwood Inference is running a focused FP8/INT8 benchmarking sprint to improve end-to-end serving performance. Microbench wins do not always translate to serving wins due to scheduler effects (continuous batching, prefill/decode interleaving), launch overhead, and variance.\\n\\nWe need:\\n1) A **deterministic and explainable** selection policy (so perf changes are attributable and reversible)\\n2) **Guardrails** to avoid correctness regressions and p95 latency regressions during rollout\\n3) A policy compatible with our hosted catalog, including model-specific quality constraints (Applied ML sign-off)\\n\\n### Goals\\n- Improve throughput (tokens/s) and/or reduce p50/p95 latency (TTFT, TPOT) on top hosted models\\n- Preserve output quality within agreed bounds (per Applied ML policy)\\n- Keep failures safe: automatic fallback to baseline kernels\\n\\n### Non-goals\\n- Designing a general-purpose autotuner. This ADR defines deterministic heuristics + minimal runtime probes.\\n- Changing model formats or introducing new quantization schemes beyond FP8/INT8 kernels supported by the runtime.\\n\\n## Definitions\\n- **Baseline:** Current BF16/FP16 kernel path (non-quantized) used when FP8/INT8 is not selected or not eligible.\\n- **FP8 path:** Quantized kernel path using FP8 (E4M3/E5M2 as supported) primarily targeting Hopper (H100).\\n- **INT8 path:** Quantized kernel path using INT8 (weight-only or activation-aware depending on kernel) supported on a subset of GPUs and shapes.\\n- **Prefill:** Prompt processing; typically longer sequence lengths and higher arithmetic intensity.\\n- **Decode:** Token-by-token generation; typically short sequence lengths per step, sensitive to launch overhead and KV cache behavior.\\n- **d_head:** Attention head dimension.\\n\\n## Decision\\n### 1) High-level selection order\\nThe runtime selects kernels **per operator group** (attention + GEMMs) with the following preference order, subject to eligibility:\\n\\n**H100 (Hopper):**\\n1. FP8 (preferred for prefill and long-context attention when eligible)\\n2. INT8 (preferred for specific GEMMs where FP8 is not eligible or shows regressions)\\n3. Baseline\\n\\n**A100 (Ampere):**\\n1. INT8 (limited eligibility; primarily GEMMs; attention remains baseline unless explicitly enabled)\\n2. Baseline\\n\\n**L4 (Ada) / cost-focused SKUs:**\\n1. INT8 (only for explicitly supported GEMM shapes; conservative defaults)\\n2. Baseline\\n\\nRationale: Benchmarking indicates FP8 provides the strongest wins on Hopper for arithmetic-heavy regimes, while INT8 can be beneficial for select matmuls on non-Hopper but has higher quality and shape sensitivity.\\n\\n### 2) Regime classifier (prefill vs decode)\\nWe classify each request step using runtime-known sequence-lengths:\\n- **Prefill regime:** input sequence length (S_in) >= 128 OR prefill tokens computed > 0\\n- **Decode regime:** per-step decode (S_step) <= 32 and prefill tokens == 0\\n\\nAdditional buckets used by heuristics:\\n- **Short context:** max(S_in, S_total) < 2k\\n- **Long context:** max(S_in, S_total) >= 2k\\n\\nNotes:\\n- Thresholds are intentionally coarse to avoid flapping and to keep behavior stable across small request variations.\\n- We allow configuration overrides per model via registry/flags (see Rollout).\\n\\n### 3) Shape-based eligibility guardrails\\nQuantized kernels are only eligible when **all** relevant shape constraints are satisfied.\\n\\n#### Common constraints (all quantized paths)\\n- Hidden size (H) must be a multiple of 128.\\n- d_head must be in {64, 80, 96, 128}. (Other head dims are baseline-only until validated.)\\n- KV cache alignment must meet runtime requirements (see Guardrails). If alignment cannot be guaranteed, fallback to baseline.\\n\\n#### FP8-specific constraints (H100)\\n- FP8 attention requires d_head in {64, 128} for default-on eligibility.\\n- FP8 attention for d_head=80/96 is allowed only under explicit allowlist flag due to observed TTFT sensitivity in mixed workloads.\\n- For long-context (>= 8k), FP8 attention is only eligible if the model\\u2019s quantization profile is marked **long_ctx_ok=true** by Applied ML.\\n\\n#### INT8-specific constraints\\n- INT8 GEMM kernels require K dimension multiple of 64 and N dimension multiple of 128.\\n- INT8 is disabled for very small GEMMs (e.g., N < 1024) where launch overhead dominates and benchmarks showed regressions.\\n\\n### 4) Concrete kernel-selection rules\\n#### 4.1 Attention (QK/V + softmax + output projection)\\n**H100:**\\n- **Prefill, short context (<2k):**\\n  - Use FP8 attention if eligible AND batch size >= 2 OR concurrent requests >= 2.\\n  - Otherwise baseline (to avoid TTFT regressions from launch overhead for tiny batches).\\n- **Prefill, long context (>=2k):**\\n  - Use FP8 attention if eligible AND quant profile long_ctx_ok=true.\\n  - Otherwise baseline.\\n- **Decode (S_step <= 32):**\\n  - Default to baseline.\\n  - Allow FP8 decode attention only under flag and only when scheduler queue depth indicates stable batching (see Scheduler Guardrail below).\\n\\n**A100 / L4:**\\n- Default baseline attention.\\n- INT8 attention is not selected by autoselect in this ADR (may be revisited after dedicated validation).\\n\\nRationale: The sprint results showed the largest, most consistent FP8 wins in prefill (especially for medium-to-long contexts). Decode attention benefits were inconsistent in mixed workloads due to kernel launch overhead and KV cache alignment sensitivity.\\n\\n#### 4.2 GEMMs (MLP, projections, output heads)\\n**H100:**\\n- Prefer FP8 GEMM for MLP/projections when eligible, except:\\n  - For decode steps with very small batch (effective M <= 4), prefer baseline unless the INT8 kernel is explicitly validated and faster for that shape.\\n- Allow INT8 GEMM as a secondary option when FP8 is ineligible (shape) or fails a correctness check.\\n\\n**A100:**\\n- Prefer INT8 GEMM when eligible and when model profile indicates eval sign-off.\\n- Otherwise baseline.\\n\\n**L4:**\\n- Prefer INT8 GEMM only for allowlisted models/shapes with demonstrated end-to-end wins.\\n- Otherwise baseline.\\n\\n### 5) Fallback rules (hard requirements)\\nThe runtime must always be able to fall back to baseline safely.\\n\\nFallback to baseline occurs when any of the following is true:\\n1. **Unsupported shape** (fails guardrails)\\n2. **Kernel execution error** (CUDA error, illegal memory access, runtime assertion)\\n3. **Correctness sentinel failure** (see Guardrails: lightweight checks)\\n4. **Perf canary rollback active** for (model, region, GPU SKU, kernel_mode)\\n5. **Quality gate not satisfied** (model profile requires eval sign-off and sign-off is missing/expired)\\n\\nImplementation requirement: the fallback must be **operator-local** (e.g., attention can fall back without disabling GEMM quantization) and must be observable via metrics tags.\\n\\n## Guardrails\\n### A) Correctness guardrails\\n- **Deterministic numerical sentinels:** For a small, fixed set of shapes per GPU SKU, run a low-cost check in CI and in pre-production canary:\\n  - Compare quantized vs baseline outputs with tolerances appropriate for FP8/INT8 (operator-level relative error bounds).\\n  - Validate no NaNs/Infs in attention scores and outputs.\\n- **KV cache alignment checks:** Enforce alignment at allocation time and validate on kernel entry. If misalignment is detected, fallback to baseline for that request step.\\n\\n### B) Performance guardrails\\n- **No TTFT regression policy for decode-dominant endpoints:** Default decode attention remains baseline unless explicitly enabled per model.\\n- **Scheduler interaction guardrail:** FP8 attention in decode is only eligible if queue depth and batch formation are stable:\\n  - Example: if prefill queue depth > threshold or if prefill/decode interleaving ratio indicates high churn, keep baseline for decode attention.\\n  - (Exact thresholds are owned by Serving Runtime Scheduling; this ADR requires the gate to exist.)\\n\\n### C) Observability and attribution\\nAll relevant metrics must be tagged with:\\n- model_id / model_version\\n- gpu_sku (h100/a100/l4)\\n- kernel_mode (baseline/fp8/int8)\\n- op_group (attention/gemm)\\n\\nMinimum dashboard slices required for rollout:\\n- TTFT p50/p95, TPOT p50/p95\\n- tokens/s per replica and per GPU\\n- error rate (5xx), CUDA error counters\\n- fallback rate (quantized->baseline)\\n\\n## Rollout plan\\n### Phase 0: Implementation behind flags\\n- Add kernel-mode flags at runtime:\\n  - `runtime.kernel_mode_attention = {baseline|fp8|auto}`\\n  - `runtime.kernel_mode_gemm = {baseline|fp8|int8|auto}`\\n  - `runtime.kernel_autoselect_enabled = true/false`\\n- Add model-registry policy fields:\\n  - `quant_profile_default = baseline|fp8|int8`\\n  - `requires_eval_signoff = true/false`\\n  - `long_ctx_ok = true/false`\\n\\n### Phase 1: Perf canary (hosted)\\n- Canary cohorts: 1\\u20135% of hosted traffic for selected (model, region) pairs.\\n- Primary regions: start with one low-blast-radius region, then expand.\\n- Rollback triggers (per cohort):\\n  - TTFT p95 regression > agreed threshold vs baseline for 30 minutes (noise-suppressed)\\n  - TPOT p95 regression > agreed threshold\\n  - CUDA error counter increase above threshold\\n  - Fallback rate spikes indicating instability\\n\\n### Phase 2: Staged expansion\\n- Expand coverage by GPU SKU:\\n  1) H100 (prefill FP8 first)\\n  2) A100 (INT8 GEMM allowlisted)\\n  3) L4 (INT8 GEMM narrow allowlist)\\n\\n### Phase 3: Default enablement\\nDefault-on requires:\\n- Benchmark matrix coverage for top hosted models on H100/A100\\n- CI smoke checks green for quantized kernels\\n- Applied ML sign-off for models marked `requires_eval_signoff=true`\\n- SRE sign-off on dashboards/alerts and a completed rollback drill\\n\\n## Alternatives considered\\n1) **Global default FP8 for H100 (all ops, all regimes):** Rejected due to observed TTFT regressions in decode/mixed workloads and long-context quality risk for certain model families.\\n2) **Pure autotuning at runtime:** Rejected for near-term due to complexity, risk of flapping, and difficulty of attribution during incidents.\\n3) **Per-model static configuration only (no autoselect):** Rejected because it does not adapt to request regimes (prefill vs decode) and leads to either leaving performance on the table or taking unnecessary risk.\\n\\n## Consequences\\n### Positive\\n- Predictable, explainable kernel selection\\n- Guardrails ensure safe fallbacks and controllable rollout\\n- Enables performance transparency claims grounded in reproducible policy\\n\\n### Negative / Trade-offs\\n- Heuristics may miss some wins for niche shapes/workloads until expanded\\n- Conservative decode policy may delay some potential decode improvements\\n- Requires ongoing maintenance of allowlists and shape constraints\\n\\n## Implementation notes (requirements)\\n- Autoselect must be computed per request step using request metadata available in the scheduler/runtime.\\n- Selection decisions must be logged at debug level (sampled) and surfaced via metrics tags.\\n- Fallback must be immediate and must not crash the worker process.\\n\\n## Open questions / follow-ups\\n1) Evaluate enabling FP8 decode attention for specific models after scheduler tuning stabilizes batching (owner: Sofia Ivanova).\\n2) Expand FP8 attention eligibility to d_head=80/96 after additional TTFT-focused benchmarking (owner: Hiro Tanaka).\\n3) Determine whether we should introduce a \\u201ctiny-batch decode\\u201d specialized path to reduce launch overhead (owner: Grace Kim).\\n\\n## Approvals\\n- Kernel selection policy: Hiro Tanaka\\n- Scheduling guardrail requirements: Sofia Ivanova\\n- Benchmark methodology sign-off: Claire Dubois\\n- Quality gating and sign-off criteria: Jonas Weber\\n- Rollout/rollback requirements: Rafael Mendes\\n\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"body\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_b188c049f6a640609ec88799d75fdc01\"\n}",

{
  "title": "ADR-019: FP8/INT8 kernel auto-selection heuristics (Hosted Runtime)",
  "space": "architecture-and-standards",
  "author": "Noah Patel",
  "owner_team": "engineering",
  "status": "published",
  "created_at": "2026-02-14",
  "last_updated": "2026-02-26",
  "reviewers": [
    "Hiro Tanaka",
    "Sofia Ivanova",
    "Rina Kobayashi",
    "Jonas Weber",
    "Claire Dubois",
    "Rafael Mendes",
    "Allison Grant"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "adr",
    "serving-runtime",
    "kernels",
    "fp8",
    "int8",
    "autoselect",
    "performance",
    "rollout"
  ],
  "confidentiality": "internal",
  "related_pages": [
    "confluence://eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/kernel-benchmarking-methodology-top-hosted-models",
    "confluence://applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles/fp8-int8-profile-policy-for-hosted-catalog",
    "confluence://eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/perf-canary-rollout-for-new-kernels",
    "confluence://architecture-and-standards/performance-standards/benchmarking-standards-fp8-int8",
    "linear://ENG-7430-kernel-auto-selection-heuristics-implementation",
    "linear://ENG-7426-perf-canary-thresholds-for-fp8-int8-rollout"
  ],
  "body": "## Status
**Accepted** (implemented behind flags; default-on gated by perf canary and eval sign-off).

## Summary
This ADR defines the runtime’s **kernel auto-selection heuristics** for choosing **FP8**, **INT8**, or **baseline (BF16/FP16)** kernel paths for attention and GEMMs during LLM inference. The heuristics are driven by:
- **GPU architecture** (H100/Hopper, A100/Ampere, L4/Ada where applicable)
- **Model shape** (hidden size, head dim, KV head dim, alignment constraints)
- **Sequence-length regime** (prefill vs decode; short vs long context)
- **Workload characteristics** (batch size, concurrency, and prefill/decode mix)

The decision includes:
- A prioritized selection order per GPU + workload regime
- Explicit **shape guardrails** (alignment, min/max dimensions)
- **Fallback rules** (correctness, unsupported shapes, quality gating)
- Rollout controls (flags, canary cohorts, and rollback triggers)

## Context
Redwood Inference is running a focused FP8/INT8 benchmarking sprint to improve end-to-end serving performance. Microbench wins do not always translate to serving wins due to scheduler effects (continuous batching, prefill/decode interleaving), launch overhead, and variance.

We need:
1) A **deterministic and explainable** selection policy (so perf changes are attributable and reversible)
2) **Guardrails** to avoid correctness regressions and p95 latency regressions during rollout
3) A policy compatible with our hosted catalog, including model-specific quality constraints (Applied ML sign-off)

### Goals
- Improve throughput (tokens/s) and/or reduce p50/p95 latency (TTFT, TPOT) on top hosted models
- Preserve output quality within agreed bounds (per Applied ML policy)
- Keep failures safe: automatic fallback to baseline kernels

### Non-goals
- Designing a general-purpose autotuner. This ADR defines deterministic heuristics + minimal runtime probes.
- Changing model formats or introducing new quantization schemes beyond FP8/INT8 kernels supported by the runtime.

## Definitions
- **Baseline:** Current BF16/FP16 kernel path (non-quantized) used when FP8/INT8 is not selected or not eligible.
- **FP8 path:** Quantized kernel path using FP8 (E4M3/E5M2 as supported) primarily targeting Hopper (H100).
- **INT8 path:** Quantized kernel path using INT8 (weight-only or activation-aware depending on kernel) supported on a subset of GPUs and shapes.
- **Prefill:** Prompt processing; typically longer sequence lengths and higher arithmetic intensity.
- **Decode:** Token-by-token generation; typically short sequence lengths per step, sensitive to launch overhead and KV cache behavior.
- **d_head:** Attention head dimension.

## Decision
### 1) High-level selection order
The runtime selects kernels **per operator group** (attention + GEMMs) with the following preference order, subject to eligibility:

**H100 (Hopper):**
1. FP8 (preferred for prefill and long-context attention when eligible)
2. INT8 (preferred for specific GEMMs where FP8 is not eligible or shows regressions)
3. Baseline

**A100 (Ampere):**
1. INT8 (limited eligibility; primarily GEMMs; attention remains baseline unless explicitly enabled)
2. Baseline

**L4 (Ada) / cost-focused SKUs:**
1. INT8 (only for explicitly supported GEMM shapes; conservative defaults)
2. Baseline

Rationale: Benchmarking indicates FP8 provides the strongest wins on Hopper for arithmetic-heavy regimes, while INT8 can be beneficial for select matmuls on non-Hopper but has higher quality and shape sensitivity.

### 2) Regime classifier (prefill vs decode)
We classify each request step using runtime-known sequence-lengths:
- **Prefill regime:** input sequence length (S_in) >= 128 OR prefill tokens computed > 0
- **Decode regime:** per-step decode (S_step) <= 32 and prefill tokens == 0

Additional buckets used by heuristics:
- **Short context:** max(S_in, S_total) < 2k
- **Long context:** max(S_in, S_total) >= 2k

Notes:
- Thresholds are intentionally coarse to avoid flapping and to keep behavior stable across small request variations.
- We allow configuration overrides per model via registry/flags (see Rollout).

### 3) Shape-based eligibility guardrails
Quantized kernels are only eligible when **all** relevant shape constraints are satisfied.

#### Common constraints (all quantized paths)
- Hidden size (H) must be a multiple of 128.
- d_head must be in {64, 80, 96, 128}. (Other head dims are baseline-only until validated.)
- KV cache alignment must meet runtime requirements (see Guardrails). If alignment cannot be guaranteed, fallback to baseline.

#### FP8-specific constraints (H100)
- FP8 attention requires d_head in {64, 128} for default-on eligibility.
- FP8 attention for d_head=80/96 is allowed only under explicit allowlist flag due to observed TTFT sensitivity in mixed workloads.
- For long-context (>= 8k), FP8 attention is only eligible if the model’s quantization profile is marked **long_ctx_ok=true** by Applied ML.

#### INT8-specific constraints
- INT8 GEMM kernels require K dimension multiple of 64 and N dimension multiple of 128.
- INT8 is disabled for very small GEMMs (e.g., N < 1024) where launch overhead dominates and benchmarks showed regressions.

### 4) Concrete kernel-selection rules
#### 4.1 Attention (QK/V + softmax + output projection)
**H100:**
- **Prefill, short context (<2k):**
  - Use FP8 attention if eligible AND batch size >= 2 OR concurrent requests >= 2.
  - Otherwise baseline (to avoid TTFT regressions from launch overhead for tiny batches).
- **Prefill, long context (>=2k):**
  - Use FP8 attention if eligible AND quant profile long_ctx_ok=true.
  - Otherwise baseline.
- **Decode (S_step <= 32):**
  - Default to baseline.
  - Allow FP8 decode attention only under flag and only when scheduler queue depth indicates stable batching (see Scheduler Guardrail below).

**A100 / L4:**
- Default baseline attention.
- INT8 attention is not selected by autoselect in this ADR (may be revisited after dedicated validation).

Rationale: The sprint results showed the largest, most consistent FP8 wins in prefill (especially for medium-to-long contexts). Decode attention benefits were inconsistent in mixed workloads due to kernel launch overhead and KV cache alignment sensitivity.

#### 4.2 GEMMs (MLP, projections, output heads)
**H100:**
- Prefer FP8 GEMM for MLP/projections when eligible, except:
  - For decode steps with very small batch (effective M <= 4), prefer baseline unless the INT8 kernel is explicitly validated and faster for that shape.
- Allow INT8 GEMM as a secondary option when FP8 is ineligible (shape) or fails a correctness check.

**A100:**
- Prefer INT8 GEMM when eligible and when model profile indicates eval sign-off.
- Otherwise baseline.

**L4:**
- Prefer INT8 GEMM only for allowlisted models/shapes with demonstrated end-to-end wins.
- Otherwise baseline.

### 5) Fallback rules (hard requirements)
The runtime must always be able to fall back to baseline safely.

Fallback to baseline occurs when any of the following is true:
1. **Unsupported shape** (fails guardrails)
2. **Kernel execution error** (CUDA error, illegal memory access, runtime assertion)
3. **Correctness sentinel failure** (see Guardrails: lightweight checks)
4. **Perf canary rollback active** for (model, region, GPU SKU, kernel_mode)
5. **Quality gate not satisfied** (model profile requires eval sign-off and sign-off is missing/expired)

Implementation requirement: the fallback must be **operator-local** (e.g., attention can fall back without disabling GEMM quantization) and must be observable via metrics tags.

## Guardrails
### A) Correctness guardrails
- **Deterministic numerical sentinels:** For a small, fixed set of shapes per GPU SKU, run a low-cost check in CI and in pre-production canary:
  - Compare quantized vs baseline outputs with tolerances appropriate for FP8/INT8 (operator-level relative error bounds).
  - Validate no NaNs/Infs in attention scores and outputs.
- **KV cache alignment checks:** Enforce alignment at allocation time and validate on kernel entry. If misalignment is detected, fallback to baseline for that request step.

### B) Performance guardrails
- **No TTFT regression policy for decode-dominant endpoints:** Default decode attention remains baseline unless explicitly enabled per model.
- **Scheduler interaction guardrail:** FP8 attention in decode is only eligible if queue depth and batch formation are stable:
  - Example: if prefill queue depth > threshold or if prefill/decode interleaving ratio indicates high churn, keep baseline for decode attention.
  - (Exact thresholds are owned by Serving Runtime Scheduling; this ADR requires the gate to exist.)

### C) Observability and attribution
All relevant metrics must be tagged with:
- model_id / model_version
- gpu_sku (h100/a100/l4)
- kernel_mode (baseline/fp8/int8)
- op_group (attention/gemm)

Minimum dashboard slices required for rollout:
- TTFT p50/p95, TPOT p50/p95
- tokens/s per replica and per GPU
- error rate (5xx), CUDA error counters
- fallback rate (quantized->baseline)

## Rollout plan
### Phase 0: Implementation behind flags
- Add kernel-mode flags at runtime:
  - `runtime.kernel_mode_attention = {baseline|fp8|auto}`
  - `runtime.kernel_mode_gemm = {baseline|fp8|int8|auto}`
  - `runtime.kernel_autoselect_enabled = true/false`
- Add model-registry policy fields:
  - `quant_profile_default = baseline|fp8|int8`
  - `requires_eval_signoff = true/false`
  - `long_ctx_ok = true/false`

### Phase 1: Perf canary (hosted)
- Canary cohorts: 1–5% of hosted traffic for selected (model, region) pairs.
- Primary regions: start with one low-blast-radius region, then expand.
- Rollback triggers (per cohort):
  - TTFT p95 regression > agreed threshold vs baseline for 30 minutes (noise-suppressed)
  - TPOT p95 regression > agreed threshold
  - CUDA error counter increase above threshold
  - Fallback rate spikes indicating instability

### Phase 2: Staged expansion
- Expand coverage by GPU SKU:
  1) H100 (prefill FP8 first)
  2) A100 (INT8 GEMM allowlisted)
  3) L4 (INT8 GEMM narrow allowlist)

### Phase 3: Default enablement
Default-on requires:
- Benchmark matrix coverage for top hosted models on H100/A100
- CI smoke checks green for quantized kernels
- Applied ML sign-off for models marked `requires_eval_signoff=true`
- SRE sign-off on dashboards/alerts and a completed rollback drill

## Alternatives considered
1) **Global default FP8 for H100 (all ops, all regimes):** Rejected due to observed TTFT regressions in decode/mixed workloads and long-context quality risk for certain model families.
2) **Pure autotuning at runtime:** Rejected for near-term due to complexity, risk of flapping, and difficulty of attribution during incidents.
3) **Per-model static configuration only (no autoselect):** Rejected because it does not adapt to request regimes (prefill vs decode) and leads to either leaving performance on the table or taking unnecessary risk.

## Consequences
### Positive
- Predictable, explainable kernel selection
- Guardrails ensure safe fallbacks and controllable rollout
- Enables performance transparency claims grounded in reproducible policy

### Negative / Trade-offs
- Heuristics may miss some wins for niche shapes/workloads until expanded
- Conservative decode policy may delay some potential decode improvements
- Requires ongoing maintenance of allowlists and shape constraints

## Implementation notes (requirements)
- Autoselect must be computed per request step using request metadata available in the scheduler/runtime.
- Selection decisions must be logged at debug level (sampled) and surfaced via metrics tags.
- Fallback must be immediate and must not crash the worker process.

## Open questions / follow-ups
1) Evaluate enabling FP8 decode attention for specific models after scheduler tuning stabilizes batching (owner: Sofia Ivanova).
2) Expand FP8 attention eligibility to d_head=80/96 after additional TTFT-focused benchmarking (owner: Hiro Tanaka).
3) Determine whether we should introduce a “tiny-batch decode” specialized path to reduce launch overhead (owner: Grace Kim).

## Approvals
- Kernel selection policy: Hiro Tanaka
- Scheduling guardrail requirements: Sofia Ivanova
- Benchmark methodology sign-off: Claire Dubois
- Quality gating and sign-off criteria: Jonas Weber
- Rollout/rollback requirements: Rafael Mendes

{
  "document": {
    "id": "dsid_8b93eef726fe48c587b20e2d806261c2",
    "path": "/knowledge/company/sources/confluence/eng-private-deployments/upgrade-and-rollback/automated-sla-driven-canary-and-rollback-cookbook-2026.json",
    "title": "Automated SLA-driven Canary and Rollback Cookbook",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/confluence",
    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"Automated SLA-driven Canary and Rollback Cookbook\",\n  \"space\": \"eng-private-deployments\",\n  \"author\": \"Priya Nair\",\n  \"owner_team\": \"engineering\",\n  \"status\": \"published\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-02-18\",\n  \"last_updated\": \"2026-08-11\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Evan Parker\",\n    \"Lina G\\u00f3mez\",\n    \"Arjun Patel\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"canary\",\n    \"rollback\",\n    \"slo\",\n    \"observability\",\n    \"runbook\"\n  ],\n  \"related_pages\": [\n    \"/confluence/eng-private-deployments/upgrade-and-rollback/incremental-stateful-upgrade-strategy-2027\",\n    \"/confluence/eng-private-deployments/day-2-ops/steady-state-ops-and-cost-optimization-playbook-2026\"\n  ],\n  \"confidentiality\": \"internal\",\n  \"body\": \"Summary:\\\\nThis cookbook defines an automated, SLA-driven canary strategy and corresponding rollback actions for private Redwood deployments (VPC and on-prem). It codifies signal aggregation, thresholds, and deterministic rollback sequencing so operators, SREs, and field engineers can run safe progressive rollouts and rely on automated protection when service-level objectives are violated.\\\\n\\\\nPurpose and scope:\\\\n- Purpose: Reduce human error during progressive rollouts by tying automated rollouts and rollbacks to observable SLAs and composite health signals.\\\\n- Scope: Applies to control-plane and model-serving releases for private deployments delivered via the Redwood operator (both VPC-managed and on-prem images). This document covers the canary policy, metric signals, decision logic, automated actions, manual escalation steps, and postmortem data collection.\\\\n\\\\nBackground:\\\\nMany incidents during upgrades are caused by subtle degradations (inference latency tails, increased token error rates, KV cache regressions) that are not visible from single metrics. Our approach combines multiple signals into a composite \\\\\\\"canary health score\\\\\\\" and enforces deterministic rollback/mitigation steps when score crosses configured thresholds.\\\\n\\\\nOwners and roles:\\\\n- Release owner: Product or Owner of the release (listed in release metadata).\\\\n- Canary executor (automation): eng-platform/canary-service (owned by the Runtime team).\\\\n- On-call SRE: eng-sre oncall rotation.\\\\n- Field operator: On-prem deployment engineer (customer-facing).\\\\n- Incident commander: assigned per incident matrix.\\\\n\\\\nHigh-level flow (summary):\\\\n1. Create canary release with metadata and small percentage routing (default 3%).\\\\n2. Start 30-minute observation window (configurable).\\\\n3. Collect signals (latency, error rate, quality evals, resource signals).\\\\n4. Calculate canary health score every 60s.\\\\n5. If score drops below yellow threshold -> partial mitigation (throttle, route to fallback model).\\\\n6. If score drops below red threshold or sustained degradation for X minutes -> automated rollback to previous model/release; notify stakeholders and create incident.\\\\n\\\\nCanary policy configuration (example YAML):\\\\n- policy_name: sla-driven-canary-2026\\\\n- rollout_percentages: [3, 10, 30, 70, 100]\\\\n- observation_window: 30m\\\\n- evaluation_interval: 60s\\\\n- thresholds:\\\\n  - green: score >= 0.90\\\\n  - yellow: 0.80 <= score < 0.90 (automated mitigation)\\\\n  - red: score < 0.80 (automated rollback)\\\\n- persistence: if any red occurs for >= 3 consecutive intervals -> rollback\\\\n\\\\nSample policy snippet (for operator):\\\\n---\\\\ncanary_policy:\\\\n  name: sla-driven-canary-2026\\\\n  rollout_steps: [3, 10, 30, 70, 100]\\\\n  observation_window: \\\\\\\"30m\\\\\\\"\\\\n  eval_interval: \\\\\\\"60s\\\\\\\"\\\\n  thresholds:\\\\n    green: 0.90\\\\n    yellow: 0.80\\\\n    red: 0.80\\\\n  rollforward_condition: \\\\\\\"all steps green for two consecutive windows\\\\\\\"\\\\n  rollback_condition: \\\\\\\"red for 3 consecutive intervals or sustained yellow for 4 intervals\\\\\\\"\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\nSignals used (metrics and derived signals):\\\\n1. latency_p95_ms (service: inference-runtime) \\u2014 95th percentile latency in ms per request.\\\\n2. latency_p99_ms \\u2014 99th percentile latency, used for tail SLOs.\\\\n3. token_error_rate \\u2014 fraction of requests with generation truncation, EOS anomalies, or abrupt stream termination.\\\\n4. kv_cache_hit_rate \\u2014 prefix cache hit rate; sudden drop indicates cache incompatibility or model mapping errors.\\\\n5. gpu_utilization_pct \\u2014 GPU utilization at canary nodes (to detect OOM or kernel regressions).\\\\n6. model_quality_regressions_per_1k \\u2014 automated eval harness detection of changed outputs for sampled prompt set (fuzzy match and semantic similarity).\\\\n7. infra_errors_per_min \\u2014 kube or runtime-level errors per minute (OOMKills, PodRestarts, gRPC errors).\\\\n\\\\nComposite canary health score (algorithm):\\\\n- Each signal is normalized to [0,1] with directionality (higher is better). The weighted sum produces the health score.\\\\n- Default weights: latency_p95: 0.30, latency_p99: 0.20, token_error_rate: 0.20, kv_cache_hit_rate: 0.10, model_quality_regressions: 0.15, infra_errors: 0.05.\\\\n- Adjust weights per-release in release metadata when a rollout is known to be latency-sensitive vs. quality-sensitive.\\\\nFormula (described):\\\\nhealth_score = sum(weight_i * normalized(signal_i))\\\\nNormalization notes:\\\\n- latency normalized = 1 - min(1, (observed_p95 - baseline_p95) / p95_sla_margin)\\\\n- token_error normalized = 1 - token_error_rate / token_error_sla_limit\\\\n- kv_cache_hit normalized = min(1, kv_cache_hit_rate / baseline_cache_rate)\\\\n- model_quality normalized = 1 - (regressions_per_1k / regression_sla_limit)\\\\n\\\\nAutomated mitigation steps (yellow):\\\\n1. Limit new canary traffic increase (pause rollout).\\\\n2. Route subsequent requests for 50% of canary traffic to fallback model variant (model: <current>-compat).\\\\n3. Increase telemetry sampling (eval harness samples 10x more prompts for quality checks).\\\\n4. Notify on-call and release owner via the incident channel with auto-created ticket.\\\\n5. Continue to monitor for up to observation_window; if improved, reattempt rollout; if persists, escalate to rollback.\\\\n\\\\nAutomated rollback steps (red):\\\\n1. Immediately remove canary variant from load balancer (route 100% to previous stable model).\\\\n2. If model is part of a packaged image roll, mark rollout as failed and trigger automated image revert in orchestration.\\\\n3. Scale down canary nodes gracefully and drain with a 60s grace period.\\\\n4. Create a rollback incident with prepopulated logs, Grafana dashboards, and the last 60m of sampled generations attached.\\\\n5. Run an automated post-rollback validation (smoke tests) before closing the incident.\\\\n\\\\nManual rollback playbook (when automation is disabled or inconclusive):\\\\n1. Confirm degrade with metrics in the canary dashboard (last 30m). Check latency_p99, token_error_rate, and model_quality_regressions.\\\\n2. From operator workstation: run the rollback command:\\\\n   - redwoodctl rollout revert --deployment <deployment-id> --to-version <previous-version> --reason \\\\\\\"canary health score < 0.80\\\\\\\"\\\\n3. Verify routes: control-plane route list --deployment <deployment-id> (expect 100% -> previous).\\\\n4. Scale down canary nodes: kubectl -n redwood scale deployment <canary-depl> --replicas=0 (or use redwoodctl).\\\\n5. Wait for smoke tests: redwoodctl smoke --deployment <deployment-id> (must pass before incident closure).\\\\n\\\\nEscalation matrix and timelines:\\\\n- Automated rollback triggers incident at time T0.\\\\n- 0-10m: Automation runs rollback and posts to #prod-incidents; on-call SRE paged.\\\\n- 10-30m: On-call SRE validates rollback; if rollback fails or new symptoms appear, Incident Commander assigned.\\\\n- 30-120m: Field operator engaged if on-prem network/storage behavior suspected.\\\\n- >120m: Engage Release Manager and Customer Success for customer communications.\\\\n\\\\nObservability and dashboards (required panels):\\\\n- Canary overview: health_score time-series, rollout percentage, and detected flags.\\\\n- Per-metric panels: latency_p95, latency_p99, token_error_rate, kv_cache_hit_rate, model_quality_regressions, infra_errors_per_min.\\\\n- Trailing window traces: last 500 generations with similarity-score diffs to baseline.\\\\n- Smoke test result panel (pass/fail, timestamp).\\\\n\\\\nTelemetry retention and attachments (for postmortem):\\\\n- Attach last 60m of raw request/response pairs (sampling 1 in 50 by default).\\\\n- Attach all canary node kernel traces and GPU process logs for last 30m.\\\\n- Preserve model binaries and config hash for the failed canary version.\\\\n- Retention: 90 days for incident analysis; 366 days for legal/regulatory review (if customer requests).\\\\n\\\\nTesting and preflight checks (required before enabling auto-rollback):\\\\n- Baseline collection: gather 72h of baseline metrics for the target workload.\\\\n- Eval harness: run a 2k prompt consistency check with semantic similarity thresholding.\\\\n- Dry-run canary: simulate rollout with internal test traffic to validate health_score generation.\\\\n- Chaos test: spawn a controlled pod restart and ensure automated rollback behaves as expected.\\\\n\\\\nOperator quick commands (examples):\\\\n- Start canary: redwoodctl canary start --deployment <id> --policy sla-driven-canary-2026\\\\n- Pause rollout: redwoodctl canary pause --deployment <id>\\\\n- Force rollback: redwoodctl rollout revert --deployment <id> --to-version <stable-version> --force\\\\n- Fetch canary score: redwoodctl canary status --deployment <id> --last 10m\\\\n\\\\nPost-rollback triage checklist (first 24h):\\\\n1. Collect incident artifacts (logs, Grafana, traces).\\\\n2. Run root-cause hypotheses: regression in kernels, tokenizer changes, KV mapping mismatch, quantization incompatibility, operator config drift.\\\\n3. Run targeted tests: binary diff, tokenization sampling, KV cache warmup analysis.\\\\n4. If model-quality regressions found: roll model to compatibility variant and re-evaluate.\\\\n5. Produce a short RCA and action items within 3 business days.\\\\n\\\\nConfiguration table (reference values):\\\\n- Default rollout initial percentage: 3%\\\\n- Observation window: 30m\\\\n- Evaluation interval: 60s\\\\n- Yellow threshold (health_score): 0.80\\\\n- Red threshold (health_score): 0.80\\\\n- Consecutive red intervals to rollback: 3\\\\n- Sampling rate for attachments: 1/50 (adjustable per-customer)\\\\n\\\\nSecurity and customer privacy notes:\\\\n- Attachments are sanitized: we strip customer PII and redact prompt tokens flagged as sensitive before persistence.\\\\n- Access to incident artifacts is restricted to the release owner, eng-sre, and customer success for that account.\\\\n\\\\nAppendix A \\u2014 Example incident timeline (realistic):\\\\n- 09:12: Canary started (3%)\\\\n- 09:42: health_score drops to 0.78 (2 consecutive intervals) -> automation applied mitigation (pause + fallback routing 50%).\\\\n- 09:50: score remains < 0.80 for 3 intervals -> automation triggers rollback at 09:50.\\\\n- 10:00: smoke tests pass; rollback incident created and marked resolved after RCA triage ticket opened.\\\\n\\\\nAppendix B \\u2014 Quick validation checklist for field installs:\\\\n1. Ensure time sync (chrony/ntp) on all nodes.\\\\n2. Ensure telemetry agent version >= 2.4.1.\\\\n3. Ensure KMS connectivity for image signing checks.\\\\n4. Preload KV caches (if available) using the canonical warmup job.\\\\n5. Verify redwoodctl connectivity to control plane and operator permissions.\\\\n\\\\nReferences and related docs:\\\\n- Incremental stateful upgrade strategy (internal) \\u2014 see related_pages\\\\n- Day-2 steady-state ops and cost optimization playbook \\u2014 see related_pages\\\\n\\\\nContact and feedback:\\\\n- For questions about this cookbook, open a PR against this page or ping #runtime-canary (Slack).\\\\n- Suggested improvements: adjust weights per-application; standardize canary dashboards across customers.\\\\n\\\\nEnd of document.\",\n  \"end\": \"\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"body\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_8b93eef726fe48c587b20e2d806261c2\"\n}",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Automated SLA-driven Canary and Rollback Cookbook\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/confluence\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/eng-private-deployments/upgrade-and-rollback/automated-sla-driven-canary-and-rollback-cookbook-2026.json\nConnector: confluence\nWorkspace: eng-private-deployments\n\nbody : summary : \\ nthis cookbook defines an automated, sla - driven canary strategy and corresponding rollback actions for private redwood deployments ( vpc and on - prem ). it codifies signal aggregation, thresholds, and deterministic rollback sequencing so operators, sres, and field engineers can run safe progressive rollouts and rely on automated protection when service - level objectives are violated. \\ n \\ npurpose and scope : \\ n - purpose : reduce human error during progressive rollouts by tying automated rollouts and rollbacks to observable slas and composite health signals. \\ n - scope : applies to control - plane and model - serving releases for private deployments delivered via the redwood operator ( both vpc - managed and on - prem images )",
